title: A yearly retreat
hook: a few days of retreat each year
tomorrow: Vesak, the rains, Tết: which holy days go on Mai's calendar?

segments.voice: Yesterday was a monthly check-in: month by month, the mirror and the smith. This week built rings wider than a day: a weekly sit, a quiet day, a gift, the moon, the month. Today, the widest ring of all.

A screenshot lands from Ông: he's signed himself and Mai up for the temple's retreat when she's home, a few days, phones in a basket at the door. Her first thought: am i even ready for that? Here's the odd part. The yearly retreat didn't begin as a test for the ready. In the old monastic rules, it begins with complaints about trampled crops.
screen: `PHONES IN A BASKET.` → `AM I READY?` → `IT BEGAN WITH TRAMPLED CROPS.`

segments.voice: The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells it. People grumbled that wandering monks kept traveling through the rainy season, treading on young plants and small creatures in the wet fields. So the Buddha set the rains retreat, vassa: for three months of the rains, monks stay in one place. What began as care for the farmers' fields became the heart of the monastic year: study, sitting, living together, staying put. Lay people joined in their own way, bringing food, keeping precepts, coming to listen. Vietnamese temples still keep a summer retreat, and some open a few days to lay families: sitting, walking, meals in silence. So a yearly retreat isn't an exam. It's a season of staying put, so what's been scattered all year can settle. Nobody arrives ready. You arrive. Now this week's rings, smallest to widest: begin again; every week, with others; a quiet day; every week, a gift; a day kept apart; month by month. And now, once a year.
screen: `MONKS IN THE WET FIELDS.` · `VASSA: STAYING PUT FOR THE RAINS.` · `NOBODY ARRIVES READY.` · `THE WEEK'S RINGS, SMALL TO WIDE.` · then, large: `ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit as if it's the first morning of a retreat: phone out of reach, back upright, hands resting in your lap. Let the body arrive before the mind does. Stay put for the whole sit, the way the monks stay put through the rains.
A yearly retreat: once a year, a few days of staying put, an echo of the monks' rains retreat.
Your line: once a year. Nobody arrives at a retreat ready; you just arrive. Two weeks, done.

screen: `DAY 1736 COUNTS.` → `WEEKLY, MONTHLY, YEARLY · 6 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: VESAK, THE RAINS, TẾT. WHICH DAYS WILL MAI KEEP?`

howItsDone: Monks and nuns keep the rains retreat (vassa) each year, staying in one place; lay Buddhists join by bringing food and keeping precepts, and temples and meditation centers also offer retreats of a few days for lay people, with sitting, walking and silent meals.
